claims.statement: Minimising sample multi-step forecast error loss functions in [[D19:multi-step estimators]] shrinks the dynamic parameters of univariate [[D1:SSOE state space models]] toward zero in finite samples relative to [[D2:MSE_1]], with shrinkage intensity increasing with the forecast horizon $h$ and decreasing with the sample size $T$.

checks.notes: The argument is heuristic: at the MSE_1 optimum the multi-step gradient equals s_1² times the gradient of Σĉ_j², pushing the parameters towards smaller ĉ_j where Σĉ_j² increases in them. In integrated ARIMA 'toward zero' means toward the values that make the c_j small (θ̂ → −1). The growth with h and the decline with T are supported by the simulations, not proved.

Argued, not proved: s_h² = s_1²(1 + Σĉ_j²) holds exactly only for uncorrelated in-sample residuals. Simulation confirms the effect: ETS(A,N,N), α = 0.6, T = 50, h = 10 gives mean α̂ 0.58 (MSE_1), 0.14 (MSE_h), 0.29 (TMSE, MSCE), 0.32 (GTMSE); it grows with h and vanishes at T = 2000. Much of it is mass at the zero bound; with a true α near zero MSE_h does not shrink relative to MSE_1.

checks.notes: With g = 0 all c_j are 0, so the h-step variance equals the one-step variance and there is no shrinkage term. The multi-step estimators still use a shifted or windowed sample, so they are not identical to OLS; the paper states the result without a derivation.

With g = 0 every c_j is 0 and the j-step error is the one-step error; MSE_h, TMSE and MSCE are least-squares criteria on shifted, pooled or summed observations, each linear in y and unbiased, so there is no shrinkage. It needs the regressors known over the horizon, and 'no shrinkage' does not mean the same estimates as OLS.

about.subject: D7

claims.statement: Maximising the [[D7:General Predictive Likelihood]] gives parameter estimates similar to those of the conventional one-step-ahead estimator [[D2:MSE_1]] under correct model specification.

checks.notes: Under correct specification Σ̂ ≈ s_1²Â, so log|Σ̂| ≈ h log s_1² and maximising the GPL approximately minimises s_1²: similar estimates to MSE_1, not identical, since Σ̂ equals s_1²Â only approximately and the window is T − h. Corollary 4.7's proof is an argument.

The multi-step errors are L̂ times the one-step residuals with L̂ unit lower triangular, so |Σ̂| is the determinant of the windowed residual autocovariance matrix: the GPL minimises h log s_1² plus the log-determinant of the residual correlation matrix, not MSE_1. It approaches MSE_1 only when T ≫ h (T = 2000, h = 10: sd of α̂ 0.017 against 0.013); in small samples it shrinks under correct specification (α = 0.2, T = 50, h = 10: 63% of estimates at 0 against 29% for MSE_1; α = 0.6: mean 0.469 against 0.582).

claims.statement: In an [[D1:SSOE state space model]] with independent homoscedastic errors, the covariance between the $i$-step-ahead and $j$-step-ahead forecast errors, for $1 \le i < j$, is $$\sigma_{i,j} = \sigma_1^2 \left(c_{j-i} + \sum_{l=1}^{i-1} c_{i-l}\, c_{j-l}\right),$$ with an empty sum when $i = 1$, and $\sigma_{j,i} = \sigma_{i,j}$, so forecast errors of different horizons are correlated unless every $c_j$ is zero.

checks.notes: Derived the covariance of the i- and j-step errors from η_{t+h|t} = Σ c_{h−j}ε_{t+j} + ε_{t+h}: for i < j it is σ_1²(c_{j−i} + Σ_{l<i} c_{i−l}c_{j−l}), as the statement now says (the printed (12) lacks the order of i and j, recorded as a misprint). Monte Carlo with ETS(A,N,N), α = 0.3, h = 5 agrees (0.297 against 0.3 for i = 1, j = 2).

Derived σ_{i,j} = σ_1²(c_{j−i} + Σ_{l<i} c_{i−l}c_{j−l}) for i < j, equivalently Σ = σ_1²LL′ with L_{ik} = c_{i−k}; a simulation of 400,000 draws agrees within 0.01. The model degenerates towards a deterministic level (ARIMA(0,1,1) with θ = −1), not to ARIMA(1,0,0); the paper's earlier statement that φ̂ shrinks towards zero is the right one.

claims.statement: In $ETS(A,N,A)$ with periodicity $m$, minimising multi-step loss functions in [[D19:multi-step estimators]] shrinks the seasonal smoothing parameter $\hat{\gamma}$ in a stepwise manner only when $h > m$, and faster than $\hat{\alpha}$ once $h > 2m$.

claims.statement: Under Gaussian errors, [[D3:MSE_h]] can achieve lower asymptotic parameter variance than [[D2:MSE_1]] in parameter regions where $c_j$ is close to zero, despite having higher variance in general.

definitions.definition: An additive-error linear state space model of the form $$\begin{aligned} y_t &= w' v_{t-1} + \epsilon_t \\ v_t &= F v_{t-1} + g \epsilon_t \end{aligned}$$ where $y_t$ is the observed value at time $t$, $v_t$ is the state vector, $F$ is the transition matrix, $g$ is the persistence vector, $w$ is the measurement vector, and $\epsilon_t \sim \text{i.i.d. } \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_1^2)$, with multi-step coefficients $c_j = w' F^{j-1} g$.

Conventional one-step-ahead mean squared error estimator minimising $$MSE_1 = \frac{1}{T-1} \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} e_{t+1|t}^2$$ where $e_{t+1|t} = y_{t+1} - \hat{\mu}_{t+1|t}$ is the one-step-ahead in-sample forecast error over $T$ observations.

Multi-step mean squared error estimator minimising the sample squared error at a specific forecast horizon $h$: $$MSE_h = \frac{1}{T-h} \sum_{t=1}^{T-h} e_{t+h|t}^2$$ where $e_{t+h|t} = y_{t+h} - \hat{\mu}_{t+h|t}$ is the conditional $h$-step-ahead forecast error.
Trace Mean Squared Error estimator minimising the sum of squared forecast errors across horizons $1$ to $h$: $$TMSE = \frac{1}{T-h} \sum_{j=1}^{h} \sum_{t=1}^{T-h} e_{t+j|t}^2$$
Mean Squared Cumulative Error estimator minimising the squared sum of forecast errors over horizons $1$ to $h$: $$MSCE = \frac{1}{T-h} \sum_{t=1}^{T-h} \left( \sum_{j=1}^{h} e_{t+j|t} \right)^2$$

Geometric Trace Mean Squared Error estimator introduced in this paper, minimising the sum of logarithmic multi-step mean squared errors across horizons $1$ to $h$: $$GTMSE = \sum_{j=1}^{h} \log \left( \frac{1}{T-h} \sum_{t=1}^{T-h} e_{t+j|t}^2 \right)$$

General Predictive Likelihood for consecutive observations $Y_t = (y_{t+1}, \dots, y_{t+h})'$ under Gaussian errors, whose concentrated log-likelihood is $$l_{GPL_h}(\theta, \hat{\Sigma} \mid Y) = -\frac{T-h}{2} \left( h \log(2\pi e) + \log|\hat{\Sigma}| \right)$$ where $\hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{T-h} \sum_{t=1}^{T-h} E_t E_t'$ is the sample multi-step forecast error covariance matrix.
Determinant of the sample multi-step forecast error covariance matrix, $$GV = |\hat{\Sigma}|$$ whose minimisation is equivalent to maximising the [[D7:General Predictive Likelihood]].

Pure additive local-level exponential smoothing model in the Gardner taxonomy with level smoothing parameter $\alpha$, multi-step coefficient $\hat{c}_j = \hat{\alpha}$, and $h$-step conditional variance $s_h^2 = s_1^2(1 + (h-1)\hat{\alpha}^2)$.
First-order integrated moving average model $(1-B)y_t = (1+\theta B)\epsilon_t$ with moving average parameter $\theta$.
First-order autoregressive integrated moving average model $(1-B)(1-\phi_1 B)y_t = (1+\theta_1 B)\epsilon_t$ with AR parameter $\phi_1$ and MA parameter $\theta_1$.

Pure additive local-trend exponential smoothing model in the Gardner taxonomy with level smoothing parameter $\alpha$ and trend smoothing parameter $\beta$, multi-step coefficient $\hat{c}_j = \hat{\alpha} + \hat{\beta}j$, and $h$-step conditional variance $s_h^2 = s_1^2\left(1 + \sum_{j=1}^{h-1}(\hat{\alpha} + \hat{\beta}j)^2\right)$.

limitations.statement: In finite samples with large forecast horizons $h$, multi-step estimators can over-shrink parameters toward boundary values, introducing finite-sample estimation bias and slow convergence rates.

The zero-shrinkage analytical result applies to static linear regression models without dynamic state transitions ($g = 0$) and does not transfer to dynamic regression models with autoregressive or moving-average error structures.

The equivalence between General Predictive Likelihood and one-step-ahead MSE_1 relies on correct model specification so that $|\hat{A}| = 1$; under model misspecification, off-diagonal covariances do not cancel and GPL estimates diverge from MSE_1.

The analytical derivation of GTMSE imposes a diagonal restriction setting off-diagonal forecast error covariances to zero, which does not hold in real dynamic time series processes whenever $c_j \ne 0$.

Monte Carlo simulation results are restricted to two univariate data-generating processes (ETS(A,N,N) with $\alpha=0.2$ and ARIMA(0,1,1) with $\theta=0.6$) and pure additive linear models, and numerical outcomes are reported visually via boxplots rather than tabulated summary statistics.

Empirical evaluations are limited to two individual univariate time series (Greenland Mean Surface Temperature and Air Passengers) with single fixed holdout origins rather than a large multi-series benchmark.

The limit of ARIMA(1,1,1) under multi-step estimation is not φ̂ = θ̂ = −1: there the h-step variance factor equals h. Its minimum is at φ̂ = 0, θ̂ = −1, where every c_j is zero, a deterministic level rather than ARIMA(1,0,0). Found by the independent proof check.

The switch at h > 2m rests on the misprinted coefficients of ETS(A,N,A) in Table 1; with the correct c_j = α + γ when j is a multiple of m, the pressure on α̂ always exceeds that on γ̂. Found by the independent proof check.

The efficiency comparisons are argued from the curvature of the likelihoods, not proved: under correct specification no consistent multi-step estimator has a lower asymptotic variance than the one-step Gaussian estimator, and a Monte Carlo with ETS(A,N,N) found MSCE more efficient than MSE_h. Found by the independent proof check.

TMSE is the maximum likelihood estimator when the forecast errors of all horizons are taken as independent with equal variances; what has no likelihood is TMSE with the variances the model implies, which grow with the horizon. Found by the independent proof check.

MSCE shrinks the most only for small smoothing parameters: for ETS(A,N,N) with α = 0.7 and for ETS(A,A,N) with small α and β at long horizons, MSE_h shrinks more. Found by the independent proof check.

Under correct specification the General Predictive Likelihood approaches MSE_1 only when the sample is much longer than the horizon: it minimises the log-determinant of the residual autocovariance matrix, and in small samples it shrinks (ETS(A,N,N), α = 0.2, T = 50, h = 10: 63% of estimates at zero against 29% for MSE_1). Found by the second proof check.

paper.summary: Forecasting models are sometimes estimated by minimising errors several steps ahead rather than one step ahead, which makes forecasts more robust when the model is misspecified. Why this happens had lacked a general explanation. Using a linear state space framework covering ARIMA and exponential smoothing models, this paper shows that multi-step loss functions automatically shrink dynamic model parameters toward zero in finite samples, whereas static regression parameters experience no shrinkage. Because strong shrinkage over long horizons can introduce estimation bias, the paper derives a General Predictive Likelihood, which avoids shrinkage when the model is correctly specified. It then proposes the Geometric Trace Mean Squared Error (GTMSE) estimator to moderate shrinkage. Simulations and real-data tests on Greenland surface temperatures and airline passengers show that GTMSE improves parameter efficiency over existing multi-step estimators and outperforms one-step estimation under model misspecification.

value.notes: Under correct specification Σ̂ ≈ s_1²Â, so log|Σ̂| ≈ h log s_1² and maximising the GPL approximately minimises s_1²: similar estimates to MSE_1, not identical, since Σ̂ equals s_1²Â only approximately and the window is T − h. Corollary 4.7's proof is an argument.

The multi-step errors are L̂ times the one-step residuals with L̂ unit lower triangular, so |Σ̂| is the determinant of the windowed residual autocovariance matrix: the GPL minimises h log s_1² plus the log-determinant of the residual correlation matrix, not MSE_1. It approaches MSE_1 only when T ≫ h (T = 2000, h = 10: sd of α̂ 0.017 against 0.013); in small samples it shrinks under correct specification (α = 0.2, T = 50, h = 10: 63% of estimates at 0 against 29% for MSE_1; α = 0.6: mean 0.469 against 0.582).

value.notes: The paper argues from the curvature of (29) and does not prove it. 'Asymptotic' cannot hold: under correct specification the one-step Gaussian estimator attains the Cramér–Rao bound, so no consistent multi-step estimator has lower asymptotic variance. A Monte Carlo (ETS(A,N,N), T = 100, h = 10, 400 runs) gave MSE_h a larger standard deviation than MSE_1 at α = 0.2 (0.132 against 0.075) and α = 0 (0.073 against 0.066); only TMSE, MSCE and GTMSE near α = 0 did slightly better (0.063), a finite-sample boundary effect.

about.subject: D4
about.relation: has no likelihood for which it is optimal

checks.notes: TMSE is MSCE with the cross-horizon covariances set to zero (TMSE = tr Σ̂, MSCE = 1′Σ̂1). But Gaussian errors with covariance σ²I give a concentrated likelihood maximised exactly by minimising TMSE; what holds is that no likelihood consistent with the model-implied variances s_j², which grow with j, gives TMSE (a diagonal matrix with those variances gives GTMSE). The paper says 'appropriate likelihood' and gives no proof.

TMSE is the trace of Σ̂ and MSCE the sum of its elements, so TMSE is MSCE without the cross-horizon covariances. But the Gaussian likelihood with Σ = τ²I_h concentrates to −(T−h)h/2·(log(2πe) + log(tr Σ̂/h)), maximised exactly by minimising TMSE; TMSE corresponds to a misspecified likelihood (equal variances, no covariances), which the model contradicts whenever c_j ≠ 0.
